title: Complex numbers and complex sinusoids
summary: Read a complex number in rectangular, polar and exponential form; find its magnitude, angle and conjugate; see a complex sinusoid as a rotating point; and explain why a real cosine is half a positive-frequency spinner plus half a negative-frequency one.
sourceNote: complex_sinusoids.pdf (Koo's note), the Day 4 slides, Lab 3 Q5–Q20.

sections.heading: Why this course needs a made-up number

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why complex numbers** Chapter 0 said a sinusoid is a rotating point seen from the side. The cosine is its x-coordinate; the sine is its y-coordinate. Tracking a point on a plane means tracking two numbers at once. ==Complex numbers pack those two numbers into one symbol== so you can write the *whole rotating point* as a single object — and then the formulas for Fourier analysis become one line instead of two. Koo's note: 'a single complex sinusoid captures both the cosine and sine waves at the same time.' That's the entire reason j exists in this course.
So don't think of j as 'the square root of −1' (true, but unhelpful). Think of it as **the label for the vertical axis**. A complex number x + jy is the point (x, y). That's it.

sections.heading: Complex numbers: three ways to write one point

blocks.title: Same point, three notations. Rectangular says where; polar/exponential say how far and which direction. Koo uses j (engineers) where mathematicians use i.
blocks.body:
rectangular:   z = x + jy                    x = Re(z),  y = Im(z)
polar (trig):  z = r (cos θ + j sin θ)        r = |z| = √(x² + y²),   θ = ∠z = atan2(y, x)
exponential:   z = r · e^{jθ}                 Euler:  e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ

frames.caption: Magnitude = length of the arrow from the origin = Pythagoras. Here it's exactly 1 — the point sits on the unit circle. (Lab 3 Q7: red = 1, blue = 1.)

lines: conjugate  z̄ = 1/2 − j·(√3/2)   (flip the sign of y)
frames.caption: Angle = the direction of the arrow, counterclockwise from the positive real axis. The point (1/2, √3/2) is (cos 60°, sin 60°), so the angle is 60° = π/3. (Q8.)

lines: conjugate  z̄ = 1/2 − j·(√3/2)   (flip the sign of y)
frames.caption: The conjugate keeps the real part and flips the sign of the imaginary part. Geometrically: mirror the arrow across the horizontal axis.

lines: conjugate  z̄ = 1/2 − j·(√3/2)   (flip the sign of y)
frames.caption: Mirroring doesn't change length, and it negates the angle. |z̄| = 1, ∠z̄ = −60°. (Q8: red = 60°, blue = −60°.)

blocks.md: e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ. Where this comes from is a calculus fact you don't need for this course; what you must be able to do is translate it: ==e^{jθ} is the point on the unit circle at angle θ==. Reading the symbols: the j in the exponent is what makes the exponential rotate instead of grow, θ is the angle in radians, and the result's real and imaginary parts are exactly the point's (cos θ, sin θ) coordinates. The exponential form r·e^{jθ} is then 'a point at distance r, direction θ' — polar form written compactly. Why bother with an exponential? Because exponentials multiply by adding exponents (e^a·e^b = e^{a+b}), which is about to let us pull frequency and phase apart cleanly.
blocks.slide: Euler's formula, in the circle picture

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Run `np.fft.fft()` on any recording and the array that comes back is complex numbers — `np.abs()` of it is the magnitude spectrum, `np.angle()` the phase spectrum, exactly |z| and ∠z from this section. Radio is even more literal: ##Wi-Fi, 5G, and GPS receivers sample two voltages, I and Q, which are nothing but Re(z) and Im(z) of the incoming wave## — 'IQ data' is complex numbers coming off an antenna. And every plugin that edits audio by frequency (EQ, pitch correction, denoisers) is doing arithmetic on these z's under the hood.

blocks.prompt: Convert 3·e^{jπ/2} to rectangular form, and write −2 in exponential form.
blocks.answer: 3(cos π/2 + j sin π/2) = 3(0 + j·1) = 3j. −2 has length 2 and points along the negative real axis (angle π): 2·e^{jπ}.

blocks.prompt: What is the magnitude of 3 + 4j, and its conjugate?

sections.heading: Complex sinusoids: the rotating point itself

blocks.md: Take z = r·e^{jθ} and let θ increase. The point goes around a circle of radius r, counterclockwise. That moving point is a **complex sinusoid**: z(θ) = r·e^{jθ} = r(cos θ + j sin θ). Its real part traces a cosine, its imaginary part traces a sine — ==one object, carrying both waves at once==. (Lab 3 Q9–Q10: plotted against θ it's a helix; θ from 0 to 8π = four full circles.)

- z̄(θ) = r·e^{−jθ} = r(cos θ − j sin θ) = r(cos(−θ) + j sin(−θ)) — same circle, **clockwise** (Q11: 'spirals clockwise').
- Add them: z + z̄ = 2r·cos θ. The imaginary parts cancel; you're left with a real cosine along the real axis (Q12, Q16).
- Subtract them: z − z̄ = 2jr·sin θ — a sine along the imaginary axis (Q13).
- So **r·cos θ = (r·e^{jθ} + r·e^{−jθ}) / 2**. ##A real cosine is the average of a counterclockwise spinner and a clockwise one## — that one sentence explains every symmetric spectrum you will ever plot.

blocks.caption: Euler's two spinners, frozen mid-rotation. z (blue) turns counterclockwise at +F; its conjugate z̄ (amber) turns clockwise at −F. Their imaginary parts are equal and opposite at every instant, so the sum (green) never leaves the real axis: z + z̄ = 2cos θ. Halve it and you have a real cosine — which is why a real wave always shows up at BOTH +F and −F in a two-sided spectrum, half the amplitude at each. Hover any part.

blocks.title: Substitute θ = 2πFt + ϕ, exactly as in Chapter 0. Then split the exponent with the product rule of exponents.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why this matters for every later lab** In Fourier analysis, each frequency gets ONE complex number X. Its magnitude is 'how much of this frequency' and its angle is 'what phase'. That's why Lab 4 asked for X₁ and got 'j' as an answer, and why a magnitude spectrum plots |X| and a phase spectrum plots ∠X. ==If you can read |X| and ∠X off a complex number, you can read a spectrum== — that's the whole payoff of this chapter.

blocks.title: A real cosine as two spinners
blocks.body:
Show A·cos(2πFt + ϕ) = X_F·e^{j2πFt} + X̄_F·e^{−j2πFt}, and say what X_F is.

1. Start from r·cos(θ) = (z + z̄)/2 with θ = 2πFt + ϕ and r = A.
2. Write z(t) = X·e^{j2πFt} and z̄(t) = X̄·e^{−j2πFt}, where X = A·e^{jϕ}.
3. So A·cos(2πFt + ϕ) = (X·e^{j2πFt} + X̄·e^{−j2πFt}) / 2.
4. Define X_F = X/2. Halving a complex number halves its length and leaves its angle alone.
5. Therefore **|X_F| = A/2** and **∠X_F = ϕ**. A real cosine of amplitude A shows up in a two-sided spectrum as two lines, at +F and −F, each of height A/2, with phases ϕ and −ϕ.

blocks.title: Dials on a complex sinusoid
blocks.body:
x(t) = A·e^{j(2πFt + ϕ)}, plotted as a spiral in 3D (time, real, imaginary).

1. Q14: double the frequency of e^{j2π·20·t} → e^{j2π·40·t}. Same spiral, twice as many turns per second.
2. Q16: e^{j2πFt} + e^{−j2πFt} = 2cos(2πFt). Two opposite spinners sum to a real cosine.
3. Q17: A = 10 instead of 1 → the spiral traces a circle of radius 10. Amplitude is the radius.
4. Q18: ϕ = π instead of 0 → the point starts on the opposite side of the circle: a half-cycle head start.
5. Q19: A is the **magnitude** of the vector, ϕ is its **angle**.
6. Q20: given X = A·e^{jϕ} numerically (e.g. 4·e^{jπ/2}), read A = 4 from the coefficient and ϕ = π/2 from the exponent.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Negative frequencies stop being philosophical the first time you plot a raw FFT: the mirror half of every real signal's spectrum is the clockwise spinners, which is why numpy offers `rfft` to hand you just the positive side. The complex amplitude X = A·e^{jϕ} is what a spectrogram cell actually stores before being squared into a picture — ==magnitude and phase per frequency is precisely what Whisper's front end and every vocoder consume==. And phase vocoders — the tool that slows audio without chipmunking it, in every DJ deck and transcription app — work by carefully rotating exactly these X's from frame to frame.

blocks.body: z = x + jy is the point (x, y). |z| = √(x² + y²) is its length; ∠z = atan2(y, x) is its angle; z̄ = x − jy is its mirror across the real axis. Euler: e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ, so z = |z|·e^{j∠z}.

z(t) = X·e^{j2πFt} is a point circling at F rotations per second; X = A·e^{jϕ} carries amplitude (|X|) and phase (∠X). A real cosine is (z + z̄)/2, so it appears at both +F and −F with half the amplitude at each.

blocks.prompt: A spectrum shows X = 0.354 − 0.354j at 2 Hz. What's the amplitude and phase of the cosine at 2 Hz?
blocks.answer: |X| = √(0.354² + 0.354²) = 0.5, so the cosine's amplitude is 2·0.5 = 1. ∠X = atan2(−0.354, 0.354) = −π/4, so the phase is −π/4. (This is the k = −2 line of the Day 5 slides' example.)

exercises.title: One point, three spellings
exercises.prompt: z = −3 + 3j. Write |z|, the angle θ (radians, exact), the polar form, the exponential form, and the conjugate z∗. Then: what is z · z∗?
hints: Plot it: real part −3 (left), imaginary part 3 (up). Magnitude is the distance from the origin — Pythagoras. Angle is measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis.
The classic error is θ = arctan(3/−3) = −π/4. That's the angle for +3 − 3j (fourth quadrant). Your point is in the *second* quadrant; add π: θ = 3π/4.
Conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part. z·z∗ always equals |z|² — check your magnitude with it.
solution: θ = 3π/4 (135°): second quadrant, 45° above the negative real axis.
exercises.why: Every value in a spectrum is a complex number, and 'magnitude and angle' is how you read it: magnitude is how loud that frequency is, angle is its phase. Get the quadrant wrong and your phase is off by 180° — which is the difference between a sound and its exact cancellation.

exercises.title: Why a cosine is two spinners
exercises.prompt: Starting from Euler's formula e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ, show in three lines that cos θ = (e^(jθ) + e^(−jθ))/2. Then say what this means for the spectrum of a real cosine at 100 Hz.
hints: Write Euler's formula twice: once for θ, once for −θ. Remember cos(−θ) = cos θ and sin(−θ) = −sin θ.
The mistake is trying to solve for cos by dividing. Instead, *add* the two equations — the j sin terms cancel.
e^(jθ) with θ = 2π·100·t is a point spinning counterclockwise at 100 Hz. e^(−jθ) spins clockwise — that's a *negative* frequency, −100 Hz. Half of each.
solution: e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ and e^(−jθ) = cos θ − j sin θ.
Add them: e^(jθ) + e^(−jθ) = 2 cos θ.

So a real 100 Hz cosine is half a spinner at +100 Hz plus half a spinner at −100 Hz. Its spectrum has two lines, at +100 and −100 Hz, each of height A/2. That's why Fourier spectra are symmetric for real signals.
exercises.why: This one identity is why every FFT plot of a real signal has a mirror image, why 'negative frequency' is a real thing engineers say, and why the DFT of an N-point real signal only has N/2 useful bins. Once you see the two spinners, the rest of the course stops being mysterious.
